analysis|04-06|1957|Ιδρύεται η Ολυμπιακή Αεροπορία|Olympic Airways is founded|Greece needed a strong national airline to connect the islands with the mainland and to serve international flights. After the war transport was difficult, and the need for a modern air network was pressing for the reconstruction of the economy. The founding of a national airline was linked with the need to connect the islands, which were hard to reach by other means. // The shipowner Aristotle Onassis took the initiative to found the new company, with a business strategy that combined boldness with his experience in shipping. Its founding coincided with the search for new business opportunities in Greece of the period. Flights to the islands changed the daily life of many residents and of businesses. The development of the aviation sector was linked with changes in tourism and in international connections. // Olympic Airways took over the flights and became a symbol of the country, with its distinctive logo of the Olympic rings. It was nationalised in 1975. Over time it faced financial problems and competition, and its activity later passed to a new company, which continued the flights with a different organisation. For decades the company was a basic symbol of Greek aviation progress and of the country's outward orientation.

analysis|04-07|1929|Ο πρώτος επίσημος αγώνας της εθνικής ομάδας ποδοσφαίρου|The first official match of the national football team|Football had begun to become popular in Greece at the start of the 20th century, with teams founded in towns and neighbourhoods. The Football Federation now organised the teams more systematically, so that regular championships could be held and the national team prepared. Football in Greece began in the ports and cities, among sailors, students and merchants. // The international match was the first official appearance on the international stage, and the preparation of the team was limited compared with European sides. The players often competed in an amateur spirit, but with great passion. The first international meetings were important for the organisation of the federations and the clubs. The match took place at a time when football still did not have a mass character. // The national team faced Italy B in Athens. This participation gave the team experience and strengthened the public's interest. Over the years the national team became a symbol of unity, with its finest moment being the victory in the European Championship of 2004. The history of the national team is linked with many generations of fans and with the particular moments of the country. This history is connected with the development of Greek sport.

analysis|04-07|1943|Ο Ιωάννης Ράλλης γίνεται πρωθυπουργός της κατοχικής κυβέρνησης|Ioannis Rallis becomes prime minister of the occupation government|During the Occupation the conquerors had installed governments that collaborated with them, without real independence. The Resistance had grown considerably, and the occupation authorities needed a political figure to maintain order and control of the country. The Occupation had brought famine and the collapse of the economy, and collaboration with the conquerors became the subject of intense public dispute. // Rallis took up the premiership and formed the Security Battalions, which collaborated with the Germans against the Resistance. This step further divided society, because it set Greeks against Greeks. The Security Battalions were regarded by society as a symbol of division, since they recruited Greeks. Political life was divided between the government, the Resistance and the occupying forces. // The collaboration left deep wounds. After the Liberation, Rallis was tried as a collaborator and sentenced, and the case became a symbol of the need for accountability among the collaborators of the Occupation. The trial of the collaborators was part of the post-war effort for justice. Historians still debate the motives of the collaborators and the limits of their responsibility. This period remains one of the most charged chapters of the Greek Occupation.

analysis|04-08|1820|Ανακαλύπτεται η Αφροδίτη της Μήλου|The Venus de Milo is discovered|Milos was then under Ottoman rule, and the antiquities of the islands were often discovered by chance by residents, who found them in farm fields or among ruins. Foreign diplomats and travellers showed interest in acquiring them, and the trade in antiquities was intense. The discovery of the Venus coincided with the period when Europeans were searching for ancient masterpieces for their museums. // After the discovery the statue passed into French hands, at a time when European collections sought works of classical art. The route of this work was the subject of several discussions about its origin and the circumstances of its acquisition. The finds of the island were numerous, and many foreign institutions acquired them in that period. The route of the statue from Milos to Paris is known mainly from testimonies and documents. // It was exhibited in the Louvre in Paris and became one of the most famous works of art in the world, symbolising Hellenistic sculpture. Greece later claimed its return, but the work remains in Paris. The presence of the work in Paris is today a subject of debate about cultural heritage. The Venus remains one of the best-known ancient statues in the world.

analysis|04-09|1941|Οι Γερμανοί μπαίνουν στη Θεσσαλονίκη|The Germans enter Thessaloniki|After the April invasion the German forces had advanced from Bulgaria and had broken the defence of eastern Macedonia, in an operation that combined speed and military superiority. Thessaloniki was a strategic hub, because it linked the northern borders with the interior of the country. The German advance from Bulgaria was part of the plan to take eastern Macedonia and Thrace. // The city was taken with relatively little resistance, because the Greek army of the area had been encircled and could not continue the battle in a coordinated way. The surrender of the city was a consequence of the general collapse. The Greek army of the area had smaller forces and limited supplies. The battles had delayed the advance, but in the end the encirclement was effective. // Oppression and occupation followed, with strict rules and restrictions on daily life. The occupation of Thessaloniki had tragic consequences, especially for the Jewish community, which was largely exterminated in 1943. The city's administration changed quickly, and the occupation authorities imposed their own rules on daily life. This period changed the life of a city with a multicultural tradition. The history of the city during this period has been studied extensively.

analysis|04-09|2000|Βουλευτικές εκλογές|Parliamentary elections|PASOK had governed since 1993, first under Andreas Papandreou and then, from 1996, under Kostas Simitis. This government had concentrated on entry into the euro area and on development, and public opinion demanded continuity or change depending on developments. The elections of 2000 were important, because they were decided on the continuation of economic policy and of the European course. // New Democracy, with a new leader, Kostas Karamanlis, tried to regain power, proposing an alternative course in the economy and administration. The pre-election campaign was intense and was conducted with strong disputes. The pre-election period was tense, and the party rivals accused each other of their choices. The contest focused on development, education and health. // The result was very close, with a small margin in favour of PASOK. Simitis continued the policy of entry into the euro area, which was completed in 2001, and of preparation for the 2004 Olympic Games. In 2004 New Democracy won the elections. This process strengthened citizens' trust in the institution of elections. This policy was widely discussed in Parliament and in the press.

analysis|04-10|1821|Τα Ψαρά υψώνουν τη σημαία της Επανάστασης|Psara raises the flag of the Revolution|Psara was an island with a strong maritime tradition and many seamen, who sailed throughout the Mediterranean. The inhabitants had merchant ships that could be converted into warships, which made the island important for the revolutionary struggle. Psara, a small island of the Aegean, had a population that lived mainly from the sea and trade. The island's history is linked with the maritime tradition of the region. // The island's entry into the Revolution strengthened the Greek fleet, together with Hydra and Spetses, which also had strong naval power. The cooperation of the islands at sea was decisive for controlling the supply routes. The participation of the Psariots in the naval struggle was important for maintaining the naval power of the Revolution. // The Psariots distinguished themselves in naval operations, and Konstantinos Kanaris, from the island, became famous for his fireships. In 1824 the island was destroyed by the Ottomans, with many dead and enslaved, and the tragedy of the island was a deep wound for its inhabitants. The destruction of the island in 1824 was one of the most dramatic moments of the Revolution. The contribution of the islands to the Revolution is widely recognised today.

analysis|04-10|1821|Απαγχονίζεται ο Πατριάρχης Γρηγόριος Ε΄|Patriarch Gregory V is hanged|When the Revolution broke out in the Danubian Principalities and in the Peloponnese, the Ottoman authorities held the leadership of the Orthodox responsible, since the Patriarch was also the head of the Rum millet. Gregory had publicly condemned the uprising, but this did not save him from the suspicions of the Porte. The Ottoman authorities had many means of pressure against the Orthodox of Constantinople. Differences between the Porte and the Orthodox existed already before 1821. // On Easter Sunday he was hanged at the gate of the Patriarchate, in an act that shocked the Christian world. His body remained exposed and was later thrown into the sea. The execution of the Patriarch took place on a day of great religious significance, which increased the emotion. News of the execution spread quickly in Europe and provoked reactions. // The execution provoked anger among the Greeks and in Russia and strengthened revolutionary enthusiasm. The Church honours him as a saint and national martyr, and his memory remains strong in the Orthodox tradition. The relationship of the Church with the Revolution was complex and was judged by different criteria. The Patriarch is today recognised as a martyr of the Orthodox faith and as a symbol of national endurance.

analysis|04-10|1826|Η Έξοδος του Μεσολογγίου|The Exodus of Missolonghi|Missolonghi was besieged by the Ottomans and the Egyptians, led by Kiutahi and Ibrahim, in one of the harshest sieges of the Revolution. The defenders had endured for months, but the food supplies had run out and there was no hope of outside help. The siege of Missolonghi was one of the longest of the Revolution, and the defence of the town had a considerable cost. The town had already withstood earlier sieges, which strengthened the confidence of the defenders. // The inhabitants and the fighters decided to leave the town at night and break the encirclement, in a decision that combined despair and dignity. The plan did not fully succeed, since the enemies were informed, and many were killed or captured. The lack of food and illnesses made the defence harder during the last months. The exodus was the last attempt at escape, in a situation with no other option. // The event shocked Europe, strengthened philhellenism and became a symbol of sacrifice for freedom. The memory of the Exodus remains alive in Greek national consciousness. The sacrifice of the defenders and the emotion of Europe about the events are linked in collective memory.

analysis|04-10|1896|Ο Σπύρος Λούης κερδίζει τον μαραθώνιο|Spyridon Louis wins the marathon|The marathon race was established at the first modern Games on the initiative of Michel Bréal, as a reference to the tradition of the messenger from Marathon. The Greeks very much wanted a victory in this event, which had special symbolic value for the place. Michel Bréal had proposed the marathon as a symbolic event that would connect the Games with antiquity. The distance from Marathon to Athens was about forty kilometres, which made the event difficult. // Spyridon Louis, from Marousi, ran with endurance, facing the heat and the fatigue of the course. His preparation and mental strength were decisive. Louis won at a time when athletes competed with limited means and without modern infrastructure. The recognition of the achievement was wide, and the athlete's name became linked with the country's first great victories. // He arrived first at the Panathenaic Stadium, before thousands of spectators. The victory caused enthusiasm. He became a national symbol, and his story became linked with the revival of the Olympic Games. His victory remains today synonymous with the history of the Olympic marathon. The Marathon is to this day one of the best-known events of the Olympics.

analysis|04-11|1990|Ο Κωνσταντίνος Μητσοτάκης γίνεται πρωθυπουργός|Konstantinos Mitsotakis becomes prime minister|Greece had gone through deadlocks and successive elections in 1989-1990, with coalition governments and political instability that hindered the economy. Public opinion had grown tired of constant changes and demanded stable government. The elections of 1989 had produced results without a clear majority, which led to cooperation between parties. Public opinion demanded stability after a period of successive crises in Parliament. // In the elections of April 1990 New Democracy came close to an outright majority, which opened the way for the formation of a government by Konstantinos Mitsotakis. The victory was the result of political discontent with the previous governments. The new government rested on the need for economic stability and for restoring trust. The balance in Parliament was fragile, so the government needed the support of small parties. // Mitsotakis formed a government with the support of a small majority. His governance focused on economic austerity, privatisations and stabilisation. The government ended in 1993 with early elections, which PASOK won. This government was linked with the major changes in the European economy of the decade and left a political imprint on Greek democratic life. This period was decisive for the transformation of the political system.

analysis|04-12|1204|Οι Σταυροφόροι καταλαμβάνουν την Κωνσταντινούπολη|The Crusaders capture Constantinople|The Fourth Crusade had set out with the aim of the Holy Land, but was diverted because of financial obligations to Venice and by the Byzantine political question. The crusaders needed ships and money, and Venice pressed them to turn towards Constantinople. Constantinople was the central target of the Crusade, but the campaign became a political matter. Venice gained considerable territories and commercial privileges after the capture. // A claimant to the throne asked for their help, promising financial reward and the union of the churches. This promise strengthened the decision of the campaign and exposed the political instability of Byzantium. The crusaders met resistance, and the siege already had serious consequences for the inhabitants. // After a siege, the crusaders entered the city and plundered it for days, destroying many works of art and churches. The empire was split up. The Latin State was founded, while the Greeks created successor states, such as Nicaea, Epirus and Trebizond. In 1261 Constantinople was recovered. The Byzantine population and ecclesiastical leadership experienced the capture as a deep wound. The dispute over the union of the churches affected relations between East and West for centuries.

analysis|04-12|1820|Ο Αλέξανδρος Υψηλάντης αναλαμβάνει την αρχηγία της Φιλικής Εταιρείας|Alexandros Ypsilantis takes over the leadership of the Philiki Etaireia|The Philiki Etaireia was founded in 1814 in Odessa and had difficulty finding a leader of standing, who would win the sympathy of the Greeks and of international public opinion. The choice of a leader was critical, because it would determine foreign support for the plan. The idea of a revolutionary organisation rested on the need to coordinate the Greeks of the diaspora. The choice of the leader was of great importance for the international image of the Revolution. // Ioannis Kapodistrias declined the proposal, and the leadership finally passed to Alexandros Ypsilantis. Ypsilantis, who served in the Russian army as an officer, organised the plan of the Revolution on the basis of his contacts in Russia. Ypsilantis was the son of a ruler of the Principalities and had strong relations at the Russian court. The tragedy of the Prut remained in history as a turning point for the relationship of the Principalities with the struggle. // He chose to start from the Danubian Principalities, in the hope of Russian support. In February 1821 he crossed the Prut, but the venture failed, while the Revolution continued in Greece with other dynamics. The failure at the Prut left the Philiki Etaireia to continue its planning with new initiatives in Greece.

analysis|04-13|1204|Οι σταυροφόροι κυριεύουν την Κωνσταντινούπολη|The Crusaders seize Constantinople|Constantinople was one of the largest and richest cities of the medieval world, with enormous commercial and cultural resources. Its position at the straits made it a strategic hub, which interested many powers of the era. Venice had strong economic interests in the trade of the East and wished to control the straits. The city was then one of the largest centres of trade and art in the Mediterranean. // The Fourth Crusade, strengthened by Venice, had turned towards Byzantium because of political circumstances and financial obligations. This decision changed the course of events, with long-term consequences for Hellenism. The plundering of the city lasted for days and caused the destruction of many historic buildings. // The crusaders took the city and plundered churches, palaces and collections. Byzantium lost its capital for about sixty years. The ecclesiastical and political division between East and West deepened, and the climate of mistrust persisted for centuries. The empire was definitively weakened. The later reactions of the Greeks led to tensions with the West that left traces. The return of the city in 1261 was a great national victory with symbolic value. The memory of the Crusade in Byzantine historiography is particularly intense.

analysis|04-13|1929|Η μεγάλη φωτιά στα Ταταύλα|The great fire in Tatavla|Tatavla was a district of Constantinople with a significant Greek population, at a time when wooden structures were common and fires were dangerous. The density of the houses and the narrowness of the streets made the area vulnerable. The community of the district was active, with churches, schools and commercial activities. The area had coexisted with other communities for centuries, with common commercial relations. // The fire destroyed a large part of the neighbourhood and left many residents homeless, who needed help from the community and from charitable bodies. The city services had difficulty responding to all needs. The residents found themselves in a difficult position, as the warehouses and houses were reduced to ashes. The rebuilding took time and was not always sufficient for all residents. // The community of the city, which had already decreased after the Asia Minor Catastrophe and the population exchange, was tested again. The event remained in the memory of the Greeks of the City as one of the serious disasters of the period. The fire contributed to the discussion about fire safety rules and the rebuilding of the districts. Its memory was passed on to families through the accounts of the older generation.

analysis|04-13|1944|Το ολοκαύτωμα του Κωσταραζίου|The Kostarazi massacre|During the Occupation the German forces faced guerrillas in Western Macedonia and often struck villages with reprisals, aiming to discourage help to the Resistance. The Kastoria area saw many such operations, which left deep marks on the communities. The guerrilla groups of the area had organised into small units that moved over difficult terrain. Kastoria and its region were among the main areas of activity of the armed groups. // In Kostarazi the Germans killed six civilians and burned 263 houses, leaving many families homeless. The residents found themselves without shelter and supplies in the winter that followed. The inhabitants of the village experienced the destruction as a result of the reprisals for the attacks. The process of restoring the communities after the war was slow and difficult. // The village was largely destroyed. The event is part of the reprisals against civilians and is preserved as local memory, together with other destructions of villages of the period. The extermination of the community was part of a wider policy of terror in Western Macedonia. This destruction is reflected in the testimonies of survivors and in the archives of the period. The memory of the village is honoured every year with events.

analysis|04-13|2003|Το δυστύχημα των Τεμπών με μαθητές|The Tempi school trip disaster|Tempi is a narrow pass with road traffic towards Northern and Southern Greece, and the national road at that time was often dangerous, with heavy traffic and frequent collisions. Weather conditions and inadequate signage increased the risk. The Tempi road is of particular importance for transport, since it connects Thessaly with Macedonia. School trips were a common activity, and the children travelled with trust. // Pupils were returning from a school trip when the bus collided with a lorry. The accident happened at one of the most loaded points of the road, with enormous consequences for the families of the children. The tragedy was linked with discussion about the responsibility of the competent services and the quality of infrastructure. // The accident claimed the lives of 21 pupils and shocked the country. In the discussion that followed, the problems of road safety were emphasised, and the need for better infrastructure and control. The community of Imathia experienced deep mourning, and the event reminds us how vulnerable young people are in road accidents. The memory of the young people who were lost is honoured every year by their families and associations.

analysis|04-15|1850|Η Βρετανία λύνει τον αποκλεισμό του Πειραιά|Britain lifts the blockade of Piraeus|The Pacifico affair broke out when the British subject Don Pacifico, from Gibraltar, claimed compensation for the destruction of his house in Athens. This dispute, which seemed local, quickly became a diplomatic crisis. British policy of the period considered the protection of its nationals a matter of prestige. The dispute had begun as a personal claim, which turned into a diplomatic issue. // The British government, under Palmerston, sent a fleet to press Athens for compensation. This stance provoked strong reaction in Greek society. Greece of the period had limited means to resist the pressure of a powerful fleet. The great powers followed developments closely, especially France and Russia. // The British fleet blockaded Piraeus and seized Greek ships. France and Russia protested, and the pressure led to a settlement. The episode showed the dependence of the small Greek state on the great powers and how they intervened in its internal affairs. The episode left a strong impression about the limits of national sovereignty in the Eastern Mediterranean. The matter was widely discussed in Parliament and in the press. The episode is regarded today as one of the characteristic examples of the period.

analysis|04-15|1896|Τελειώνουν οι Ολυμπιακοί Αγώνες της Αθήνας|The Athens Olympic Games end|The Games had begun on 6 April by the new calendar and had attracted athletes and spectators from Greece and abroad. The organisation had concerns about its success, because of financial and organisational difficulties. The organisation of the Games showed Europe that modern Greece could host international events. The success strengthened the country's self-confidence on the international stage. // The closing ceremony was held with the participation of King George I, in an atmosphere of enthusiasm and national pride. The organisation exceeded the expectations of many observers. The athletes competed in different events, and the audience filled the seats. The press of the period accompanied the events with extensive reporting. // The Games strengthened the international prestige of Greece and gave impetus to the idea that the institution should continue. Later the Games of Paris in 1900 and of the following cities followed, which developed the modern Olympic institution. The legacy of the organisation is seen in the continuation of the institution and in the establishment of the Games. The Games of 1896 remain in collective memory as the starting point of modern Olympism. Reference to the 1896 Games remains central in international sporting history.

analysis|04-15|1951|Οι πρώτες δημοτικές εκλογές όπου ψηφίζουν οι γυναίκες|The first municipal elections in which women vote|In Greece the right of women to vote had been discussed for decades, with politicians and movements that supported it. It had already been given in limited form in the municipal elections of 1930, to literate women, but its generalisation was delayed. The delay in generalising the right was due to political resistance and social habits. The earlier elections had a significant impact on the political system of the country. // The increased participation of women in the elections showed their interest in public affairs and in shaping local life. Women were active in neighbourhoods and social organisations. Women still had limited participation in public life, despite the changes. The participation of women in the elections of 1956 is a point of reference for the history of democracy. // The right in national elections was established in 1952, and women voted for the first time in parliamentary elections in 1956. This development is an important step towards political equality of the sexes. The vote of women strengthened their position in politics and in society. This development is part of a wider movement for women's rights in Europe. This development contributed to the gradual normalisation of political rights.

analysis|04-16|2003|Η Συνθήκη Προσχώρησης στην Ευρωπαϊκή Ένωση υπογράφεται στην Αθήνα|The Treaty of Accession to the European Union is signed in Athens|The European Union was preparing its largest enlargement, with countries of Central and Eastern Europe and of the Mediterranean. The process was complex, since it required the adaptation of the legal and economic systems of the candidates. The enlargement process was the result of the Union's wider strategy after the end of the Cold War. The candidate countries adapted their laws and administrations to European requirements. // Greece held the Presidency of the Council, and Athens hosted the ceremony, in a festive and diplomatic climate. The choice of the city had symbolic significance for European history. The signing in Athens symbolised European unity after a long process of negotiations. The ceremony in the Stoa of Attalos took place in the presence of many delegations and leaders. // Ten states signed the Treaty under the Stoa of Attalos in the Ancient Agora. Their accession took place in 2004. For Cyprus it was a major diplomatic achievement, although accession in practice concerned the areas under the control of the Cypriot government. This development changed the geography and the balances of Europe. The enlargement of 2004 is regarded as one of the most important changes in European history.

analysis|04-17|1967|Συναυλία των Rolling Stones στην Αθήνα|Rolling Stones concert in Athens|The Rolling Stones were among the greatest bands of the era and were touring Europe, with great appeal among young people. Athens was one of the stops, something rare for the country at that time, when international music was limited. The rock music of the 1960s changed the models of youth throughout Europe. The visit of foreign bands was often a subject of discussion in the press. // The concert took place at the Leoforos stadium and was an important event for young people, who saw in music a form of freedom. The atmosphere was intense and full of expectations. The reaction of authority to youth culture was often wary. The organisation of the concert required permits and coordination with the authorities. // A few days later, on 21 April, the dictatorship was imposed, which restricted freedoms and controlled culture. The concert remains in memory as one of the last moments before the junta period. The concert took place shortly before the fall of a regime that restricted collective events. The cultural life of Athens was then looking for new forms of expression. The concert remains today a subject of references in the musical history of the country.

analysis|04-18|1897|Αρχίζει ο Ελληνοτουρκικός Πόλεμος του 1897|The Greek-Turkish War of 1897 begins|Crete was in revolt against the Ottomans, and Greece sent an army and a fleet to the island, causing tension with the Sublime Porte. The revolt had strong resonance in Greek society, and the government found itself facing national pressure. The tension in Crete had political and religious dimensions, with the participation of local populations. This crisis was one of the most important of the late 19th century for Greece. // In Greece the pressure for war was great, especially from the National Society, which demanded reinforcement of Crete. The war was fought mainly in Thessaly and Epirus. The Greek fleet had sent forces to support the revolutionaries of the island. Those events also affected the country's relations with the great powers. // The Greek army, unorganised and poorly prepared, was defeated within a few weeks. The great powers intervened and Greece paid an indemnity. The defeat later led to military reforms. Crete gained autonomy. The diplomatic tension with the Sublime Porte escalated quickly during the spring. The war left many questions about the readiness of the Greek state. The Cretan crisis was linked with the national expectations of the period.

analysis|04-18|1941|Αυτοκτονεί ο πρωθυπουργός Αλέξανδρος Κορυζής|Prime Minister Alexandros Korizis takes his own life|Prime Minister Alexandros Korizis, former governor of the National Bank, took over the premiership after the death of Ioannis Metaxas in January 1941. The country was already at war with Italy, and the German attack was at the gates, which made the situation extremely difficult. Metaxas had governed since 1936 with an authoritarian regime, and his death left a vacuum of power. The course of the military operations had brought the country into immediate danger. // Korizis was responsible for a government that faced military collapse and diplomatic deadlock. His political choices were limited by the allied commitments and by the need to maintain national unity. Korizis had taken over in an extremely difficult situation, with the army in retreat. The despair of the moment was felt particularly in the capital. // As the army was retreating and the situation was becoming hopeless, Korizis took his own life. The government passed temporarily to King George II, and later to Emmanouil Tsouderos. The event shows the weight of political leadership in those critical days. The crisis of leadership in those days affected the morale of society and of the army.

analysis|04-19|1824|Πεθαίνει ο Λόρδος Βύρων στο Μεσολόγγι|Lord Byron dies in Missolonghi|Lord Byron was already one of the most famous poets of Europe and supported the Greek cause through political and financial initiatives. His poetry had deeply influenced European sympathy for the struggle of the Greeks. Byron had devoted time to the study of Greek history and language. His influence on European literature was enormous and lasting. // He arrived at Missolonghi in early 1824, with money and the intention of helping to organise the Revolution, aiming to coordinate the forces of the foreign philhellenes. His presence gave the struggle great international publicity. His presence at Missolonghi gave the Revolution major international prominence. The reaction to his death was linked also with the need to organise the Greek struggle. // He fell ill with fever and died before taking part in military action. His death caused great emotion, and the Greeks mourned him as a friend of the nation. It strengthened European sympathy for Greece and later became a symbol of philhellenism. His death remained in collective memory and still inspires the memory of the philhellenes today. His name remains linked with the philhellenic tradition of Europe.

analysis|04-20|1453|Τα τρία πλοία σπάζουν τον αποκλεισμό|Three ships break the blockade|Constantinople was besieged by land and sea, and the defenders urgently needed supplies and reinforcements. The Ottoman fleet had blocked the entrance to the Golden Horn, with chains that prevented ships from passing. The naval battle in the Golden Horn was of great importance for control of the entrance to the city. The blockade of the bay was one of the most critical aspects of the siege. // Three Genoese ships and one Byzantine, after a hard naval battle, managed to pass and reach the harbour. The success raised the morale of the besieged and caused anger in the sultan, who regarded the attempt as a threat. Genoese participation was often voluntary and based on commercial interests. The need for supplies had become urgent, as the defenders had limited stocks. // Shortly afterwards, however, the Ottomans moved ships overland into the Golden Horn, changing the balance of the siege. This move showed the sultan's ability to find solutions in difficult military situations. The history of the siege is linked with the end of the Byzantine era. The developments of the period have been widely studied by European historians. The city with its walls resisted attacks for centuries.

analysis|04-20|1941|Παραδίδεται ο ελληνικός στρατός της Ηπείρου|The Greek Army of Epirus surrenders|The Greek army of Epirus and Macedonia had fought against the Italians, but after the German attack it found itself in a difficult position, at risk of encirclement by the German divisions. The continuous advance of the enemies had left the units without adequate supplies. The Greek army of Epirus had fought hard battles with the Italians in the previous months. The position of the troops was difficult, because the supply lines had been cut. // General Tsolakoglou, commander of the Army of Epirus, signed a surrender to the Germans without initially informing the government. This decision provoked strong reactions from the political leadership and the army. The surrender caused reactions about its consequences for the government and the Resistance. The occupation government that followed was linked with cooperation with the occupation forces. // He then formed an occupation government. The surrender opened the way for the advance of the Germans towards southern Greece and became the subject of intense dispute, which continued after the war. The decision was much discussed after the war, and the responsibility of the commander remains a subject of historical research. The history of the surrender is linked with the collective experience of the first occupation period.

analysis|04-20|2000|Ο Παναθηναϊκός πρωταθλητής Ευρώπης στο μπάσκετ|Panathinaikos is European basketball champion|Panathinaikos was a strong force in Europe in the 1990s and had won the Euroleague trophy in 1996. Thessaloniki hosted the Final Four of 2000, which was a major event for the city and for Greek basketball.
